key: When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.
s: The chapter calls holding the Tao of old to direct the present, and knowing the ancient beginning, the clue of Tao; Wang Bi, on chapter 14, takes that Tao as the formless and nameless ancestor of all things, through which every age, however customs change, achieves its order, so the ancient beginning can still be known now.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 無形無名者，萬物之宗也。雖今古不同，時移俗易，故莫不由乎此以成其治者也。…上古雖遠，其道存焉，故雖在今，可以知古始也。
evidence.gloss: What is without form and without name is the ancestor of all things. Though present and past differ, and times shift and customs change, none fails to follow it in achieving its order. … Though high antiquity is remote, its Tao remains; so even now one can know the ancient beginning.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 14, at [13]). Wang Bi’s base text 執古之道，以御今之有。能知古始，是謂道紀 matches the key verse, and his comment on it says the formless and nameless is the ancestor of all things, that every time follows it to achieve order however customs change, and that the ancient beginning can be known now because its Tao remains. The sentence paraphrases these clauses without addition; plain sense restates the verse. entry-check ok.
